settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The parts.length==2 && verifiers.isEmpty() branch explicitly requires header.algorithm == Algorithm.none, and a 2-part token presented with a verifier is explicitly rejected, so the plain 'unsigned token' path is guarded
exp and nbf are always validated before a JWT is returned
RSAVerifier enforces key length >= 2048 and the HS/RS canVerify methods restrict the algorithms each verifier claims to support
No production caller other than tests is present in this repository, so effective configuration is unknown
candidates.description: decode(String, Verifier...) selects a verifier only by testing v.canVerify(header.algorithm) and then calls the shared decode(...), which passes the untrusted header algorithm straight into verifier.verify(...). Two consequences are visible in source: (a) there is no rejection path for header.algorithm == Algorithm.none when verifiers are supplied (the none case is only handled in the parts.length==2 && verifiers.isEmpty() branch, and Verifier.canVerify implementations return false for none, leaving verifier==null on the map path); (b) the algorithm used for verification is taken from the attacker-controlled token header rather than fixed by the calling application. Verification implementations then resolve the primitive by name from that value (HMACVerifier: Mac.getInstance(algorithm.getName()) / SecretKeySpec; RSAVerifier: Signature.getInstance(algorithm.getName())), and Algorithm.none.getName() returns "None", which is not a valid JCE algorithm, so it throws RuntimeException (NoSuchAlgorithmException) instead of InvalidJWTSignatureException. This is the classic 'fixed verifier + attacker-chosen alg' pattern: an application passing a single HMACVerifier and expecting HS-only acceptance has no library-side guarantee that the header says HS*, and a token with an alg the verifier cannot verify should be rejected as an invalid signature rather than flowing into verify().
missing_evidence: No application code in the repository shows how verifiers are constructed/keyed in real deployments, so it is unproven whether a strict algorithm allow-list is applied above the library

No test exercises a token whose header alg is 'none' together with a supplied verifier, nor a fixed HMAC verifier receiving an RS* header, so the runtime behaviour for these combinations is inferred from source only
Whether a caller-supplied Verifier implementation could accept an unexpected algorithm was not evaluated
preconditions: Caller uses the public decode(String, Verifier...) or decode(String, Map, Function) API and relies on the library (rather than its own allow-list) to bind the token algorithm to the expected algorithm
Attacker can submit an arbitrary JWT to the decoding application
For the alg=none case: a token with a 3-part body (header.payload.signature) whose header alg is none
candidates.title: JWTDecoder does not bind the verification algorithm to the caller-selected verifier and does not reject alg=none when a verifier is supplied (algorithm confusion at the decode boundary)

counter_evidence: The API returns the parsed issuer/audience so callers can implement their own strict comparison; the Javadoc on the claim fields documents them as OPTIONAL
exp/nbf are enforced, which limits the practical impact of a replayed token with a bounded lifetime
No in-repo consumer code was found, so it cannot be shown that any deployment omits aud/iss checks
candidates.description: The decode path validates only exp and nbf via JWT.isExpired / JWT.isUnavailableForProcessing. The JWT object exposes issuer/audience as plain fields and claim accessors (getObject/getString/getRawClaims) only read them; no library code compares the issuer or audience against an expected value, and no permitted clock skew or leeway is applied to exp/nbf. Any application that assumes the library enforces audience/issuer will accept tokens issued for another audience/issuer (token substitution) as long as the signature checks out. Timestamps are derived from Instant.ofEpochSecond(value) with no bounds checks in ZonedDateTimeDeserializer, and when exp/nbf are absent from the payload no corresponding check is performed at all.
missing_evidence: No configuration or integration artifact shows whether callers validate aud/iss; framework/DI enforcement is out of scope of the read spans
No evidence of the intended contract (whether the library is documented to validate aud/iss) beyond README examples that never set or check them
preconditions: Application consumes JWT.getIssuer()/audience/claims and does not perform its own aud/iss comparison against an expected value
Attacker can obtain or reuse a validly signed token whose aud/iss differ from the target application's expectation (e.g. a token legitimately signed for another aud by the same key/service)
candidates.title: No verification of issuer/audience (and no clock skew/leeway) in the decode path; token trust relies entirely on caller checks

counter_evidence: deserialize is called only with concrete whitelisted classes Header.class and JWT.class, and Header/JWT do not enable Jackson default typing, so a generic gadget deserialization path is not demonstrated
ObjectMapper is pre-configured only with inclusion/feature settings and a JacksonModule; no polymorphic typing is enabled in the reviewed code
The exact CVE scope/version mapping is not established from source in this repository
candidates.description: pom.xml pins jackson-databind/jackson-core 2.8.1, an old release line with multiple reported CVEs; Mapper uses a shared static ObjectMapper and the generic deserialize(byte[], Class<T>) entry point is used both for the token header and payload. README declares version 1.3.0 and carries a security notice that a vulnerability existed (CVE-2018-1000125) which 'may allow the library to incorrectly validate a JWT'. This is a version/consistency observation about the reviewed snapshot; it is not proof that any specific CVE remains exploitable in this code, and deserialization here targets fixed domain classes (Header/JWT) rather than arbitrary types.
missing_evidence: No dependency-scan report or CVE-to-version mapping is included in the repository
Whether callers invoke Mapper.deserialize with other types cannot be determined (no consumer code present)
preconditions: Deployment uses this snapshot's dependency set (jackson 2.8.1) and does not override it via dependency management
Deserialization is performed on attacker-supplied bytes (always true for the JWT header/payload)
candidates.title: Configuration/dependency observations: pinned jackson-databind 2.8.1 and README version 1.3.0 documenting a known JWT-validation vulnerability

counter_evidence: Both singletons hold no mutable state, so a racing construction does not obviously corrupt any security decision
JWT.getDecoder()/getEncoder() are thin wrappers returning the same instance; the JWT object itself is explicitly documented as not thread-safe and not to be re-used
candidates.description: JWTDecoder.getInstance() and JWTEncoder.getInstance() use the classic unsynchronized lazy-init pattern with a non-volatile static field. Under concurrent first access, two threads may observe a partially constructed instance, and distinct instances may be returned. Both classes are stateless, so the practical impact appears limited to duplicated instances and object-identity assumptions rather than token corruption; JWT itself is documented as not thread-safe.
missing_evidence: No test or documentation shows concurrency expectations for the singletons
Whether any caller mutates decoder/encoder state through the returned instance was not established (classes expose only stateless methods in the reviewed source)
preconditions: Two or more threads call JWT.getDecoder()/getEncoder() for the first time concurrently
Caller relies on a single shared instance, or on the state of the singleton
candidates.title: Static lazily-initialized non-volatile singletons for JWTDecoder and JWTEncoder (unsafe publication)

counter_evidence: RSAVerifier rejects public keys below 2048 bits, and RSAUtils throws InvalidParameterException for unknown public/private key headers
extractPublicKeyFromPEM requires the sequence length to be exactly 2 for PKCS#1 and getRSAPrivateKeySpec requires at least 9 elements
These paths affect key material / exception behaviour rather than directly reflecting untrusted request data into a sink, and no in-repo caller passes request data here
candidates.description: RSAVerifier's constructor builds the trust anchor from an unvalidated PEM string: it calls RSAUtils.getPublicKeyFromPEM(publicKey) and then reads publicKey.getModulus().bitLength() to enforce >= 2048 bits. RSAUtils.getKeyBytes and PEMUtils.decodeCertificate locate the BEGIN/END markers with indexOf and then substring without verifying ordering/absence, so a malformed or attacker-influenced key blob (e.g. a supplied certificate chain) can yield StringIndexOutOfBoundsException or a GeneralSecurityException wrapped in RuntimeException instead of a clean validation error; extractPublicKeyFromPEM also relies on String.contains to pick a format branch. The key-length gate is the security-relevant check and it is only applied in RSAVerifier, not in other RSAUtils entry points.
missing_evidence: No caller code shows whether PEM/certificate strings are attacker-controlled or only read from trusted local configuration
The behaviour for missing markers (indexOf == -1) was not exercised by any test in the repository
preconditions: Key/certificate material reaches these methods from configuration, a JWKS fetch, or an X.509 input that is not strictly validated by the caller
The public key passed to RSAVerifier is smaller than 2048 bits (rejected) or the PEM text is malformed/ambiguous
candidates.title: Non-defensive PEM/key parsing in RSAVerifier/RSAUtils/PEMUtils throws raw runtime exceptions on malformed key material

counter_evidence: Overloads that accept an explicit algorithm exist, so callers can select SHA-256/stronger
The x5t value is only a thumbprint of certificate bytes and, in the reviewed source, is not itself used to select a trusted key during verification
The digest algorithm is used to compute the thumbprint, not to decide whether to trust a certificate
candidates.description: RSAUtils.generateJWS_x5t(String, ...) overloads default to "SHA-1", and the algorithm parameter is passed directly to MessageDigest.getInstance in digest(); PEMUtils/X509 handling in extractPublicKeyFromPEM parses a supplied certificate without any chain or validity validation. SHA-1 is a weak hash for generating certificate thumbprints, and an arbitrary algorithm string is accepted (failing with IllegalArgumentException only when it is unknown).
missing_evidence: No in-repo use of generateJWS_x5t in a verification/trust path was found, so the security impact of a SHA-1 thumbprint here is unestablished
No evidence that the certificate bytes are attacker-controlled
preconditions: Caller uses the convenience overloads generateJWS_x5t(encodedCertificate)/generateJWS_x5t(byte[]) or the single-argument form, thereby getting SHA-1
The thumbprint value is relied upon as a key/certificate reference (x5t) suitable for security decisions
candidates.title: SHA-1 default for x5t thumbprint generation and unvalidated digest algorithm parameter
